intro: Greedy next-token choices can miss a stronger completed sequence. Beam search retains several partial sequences, but pruning still makes it an approximate search.
task: Compare greedy and wider-beam decoding on a transition table where a locally attractive choice can lose later.
requirements: log_probs is a finite square (V,V) matrix of nonpositive transition log scores, 1<=V<=50. Rows need not normalize because this lesson also accepts additive scoring tables.
start and eos are valid token indices, width is an integer 1..100, and max_steps is an integer 0..20. Initialize with [start] and score 0; completed EOS sequences are carried without extension.

Each step expands every unfinished beam by all tokens, then retains the best width entries by descending total score and lexicographic token-sequence ties. Return dict tokens and score for the best remaining beam. max_steps counts generated tokens, excluding start.

Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, except where a stricter bound is stated. Booleans are not numeric parameters. Leave all caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Completed hypotheses remain candidates
hints.body: Carry their score and token sequence forward without adding another transition.

hints.title: Prune after pooling expansions
hints.body: Sort all candidates together, not each parent beam separately.

explanation: Beam search trades memory and compute for a larger candidate frontier. A wider beam can retain an initially weaker branch that later becomes the best surviving sequence.

This explicit scoring variant has no length normalization, repetition penalty, or stochastic sampling. A completed short sequence can therefore outrank a longer sequence whose extra log scores reduce its total.
